In a study examining the life-history traits of the Hong Kong warty newt Paramesotriton hongkongensis under controlled laboratory conditions, researchers documented several key developmental milestones at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The incubation period from oviposition to hatching was recorded as 25 days [ab = 25 days], a duration consistent with the relatively slow embryonic development observed in the genus Paramesotriton at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The newly emerged hatchlings possessed a wet weight of 0.0128 grams [Wwb = 0.0128 grams], reflecting the modest energetic reserves stored within their gelatinous egg capsules. Following metamorphosis, the growing juveniles entered a prolonged period of somatic growth before the onset of gonadal maturation. The ultimate snout-vent length attained by adult females was found to be 7.02 centimeters [Li = 7.02 centimeters], a size that permits the accommodation of a substantial clutch volume. In contrast, adult males reached a somewhat smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 6.69 centimeters [Li = 6.69 centimeters], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism typical of many salamandrids.

Female Hong Kong warty newts undergo sexual maturation at a snout-vent length of 5.3 centimeters [Lp = 5.3 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the attainment of puberty and the onset of vitellogenesis. This size at sexual maturity is considerably smaller than the ultimate size achieved by adult females, indicating a substantial period of post-pubertal growth. Under the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at puberty was calculated to be 1,095 days [tp = 1,095 days], representing approximately three years of development. This extended juvenile phase is characteristic of relatively slow-growing urodeles inhabiting subtropical stream ecosystems. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for reproductive females is 10.8 grams [Wwi = 10.8 grams], a body mass that supports the energetic demands of egg production and amplexus. For males, the ultimate wet weight reaches 9.6 grams [Wwi = 9.6 grams], a slightly lower mass consistent with their smaller linear dimensions.

The actual fecundity in the wild is modulated by resource availability, with females laying smaller clutches during years of reduced prey abundance. This reproductive strategy, refined over evolutionary timescales, allows the species to maximize annual offspring production within the constraints of its subtropical stream habitat.

The life cycle of this species is thus characterized by a relatively extended juvenile phase, a moderately long reproductive window, and a substantial investment in individual growth. The ultimate snout-vent length achieved by females is 7.02 centimeters [Li = 7.02 centimeters], while males reach 6.69 centimeters [Li = 6.69 centimeters], confirming the pronounced sexual dimorphism.
